Data obtained under RTI by the National Campaign for Dalit Human Rights (NCDHR) in 2021 indicated that SC/ST officers constituted only 12 % of Joint Secretary-level empanelled officers and 8 % of Additional Secretary-level empanelments, against a combined quota of 22.5 %.

Promotion quotas for SC/ST in Group A services are governed by the Supreme Court's judgment in M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006), which upheld reservation in promotion subject to quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequacy of representation, and administrative efficiency. The DoPT's 2019 OM (No. 36012/16/2019-Estt.(Res.)) mandated cadre-wise review committees to generate such data. As of 2023, only 14 of 24 Group A services had completed the review, and promotion backlogs for SC/ST officers at the Senior Administrative Grade (SAG) and above persist. The 2022 judgment in Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (review of Nagaraj) struck down the "creamy layer" exclusion for SC/ST in promotion but upheld the requirement of quantifiable data, leading to further litigation in the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) and High Courts.

Caste dynamics within the services manifest in subtle exclusion: the "General Category" officers' associations have historically opposed reservation in promotion, while SC/ST officers' associations (e.g., All India SC/ST Railway Employees Association, Confederation of SC/ST Organisations) have advocated for roster-based promotion, timely DPC (Departmental Promotion Committee) meetings, and grievance redressal mechanisms. The 2018 DoPT OM on "Prevention of Harassment of SC/ST Employees" mandated a nodal officer in each ministry/department, but a 2022 survey by the Indian Institute of Public Administration found that 68 % of SC/ST Group A officers reported experiencing caste-based discrimination in work allocation, performance appraisal, or deputation opportunities.

The lateral entry scheme introduced in 2018 (DoPT OM No. 11/1/2018-EO(SM-III)) for Joint Secretary/Director level positions from the private sector and academia operates without reservation, citing the "contractual" nature of appointments. The Parliamentary Committee on Welfare of SCs/STs (2021–22) recommended extending reservation to lateral entry, but the government has maintained that the scheme is outside the reservation framework. This creates a dual-track senior leadership pipeline where the reserved category share in direct recruitment does not translate into proportional representation at the policy-making apex.

  • Assuming that the Tribal Sub-Plan/ST Component applies to the entire Union Budget rather than identified scheme-based plan allocations of participating ministries.
  • Confusing the Forest Rights Act's FPIC requirement (consent) with the Wildlife Protection Act's post-2022 "consultation" standard for relocation from protected areas.
  • Treating khap panchayats as legally recognised bodies akin to Gram Panchayats, ignoring that they have no constitutional or statutory sanction and their diktats are extra-legal.
  • Believing that reservation in the Civil Services Examination automatically ensures proportional representation at Senior Administrative Grade and above, overlooking promotion quotas, cadre allocation effects, and the lateral entry pathway without reservation.
  • Equating the NTCA's cash relocation package (₹15 lakh) with a livelihood-secure outcome, ignoring evidence of distress sales and landlessness within 3–5 years.
  • Assuming the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act covers all honour-crime victims, when it only applies if the victim belongs to SC/ST — dominant-caste victims of khap violence fall under general IPC provisions.
  • Overlooking that the 8.6 % ST population share (2011 Census) is the benchmark for STC proportionality, not the current estimated population, and that several central ministries are exempt from the earmarking norm.

Caste and the Private Sector: Corporate Diversity Initiatives, Employment Data and Regulatory Gaps

Legislative and Regulatory Framework

The Companies Act, 2013 mandates Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) spending for companies meeting specified thresholds, but it does not require disclosure of workforce composition by caste. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR) Regulations, 2015, as amended in 2021, introduced Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) which requires listed entities to report gender‑wise employee data; caste‑wise reporting remains voluntary. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) issued a 2020 advisory encouraging firms to adopt “Diversity and Inclusion” policies, yet compliance is self‑certified and not subject to audit.

Voluntary Corporate Practices

Several large conglomerates have published annual diversity reports that include caste breakdowns for the first time (e.g., a 2022 report from a major IT services firm showed 12 % SC and 4 % ST representation in its Indian workforce). Industry bodies such as NASSCOM and CII have launched “Diversity Charters” that set aspirational targets for SC/ST hiring, but these are non‑binding. The 2021 NITI Aayog “Strategy for New India @75” highlighted the absence of a statutory mandate for caste data in the private sector as a data gap for evidence‑based policy.

Judicial and Policy Developments

The Supreme Court in Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2022) reiterated that reservation under Articles 16(4) and 16(4A) applies only to public employment. No judicial pronouncement has extended reservation to private enterprises. The 2023 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Labour recommended that the forthcoming “Code on Social Security” include a provision for mandatory caste‑wise reporting by establishments employing more than 20 workers, but the bill has not yet been enacted.

Data Gaps and Research

Academic studies using the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2021‑22 estimate that SC/ST workers constitute roughly 22 % of the formal private‑sector workforce, yet they are concentrated in low‑wage, contract‑based roles. The lack of a unified employer‑level caste database hampers enforcement of the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, and the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013, for intersectional discrimination claims.

Tribal Customary Law and the Uniform Civil Code Debate: Constitutional Provisions, State Practices and Judicial Precedents

Constitutional Safeguards for Customary Law

Article 371A (Nagaland) and Article 371G (Mizoram) explicitly protect the religious and social practices of the Naga and Mizo communities, including customary law on marriage, inheritance and land tenure. The Sixth Schedule (Articles 244(2) and 275(1)) empowers Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram to legislate on matters such as marriage and divorce according to tribal customs. The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) recognises the Gram Sabha’s authority to manage community resources in accordance with customary law.

Judicial Engagement with Customary Law

In Shah Bano (1985) the Supreme Court held that Section 125 CrPC applies irrespective of personal law, but the judgment sparked a political debate that led to the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986. In Shayara Bano (2017) the Court declared instant triple talaq unconstitutional, yet it refrained from adjudicating on tribal customary divorce practices. The 2018 Law Commission Consultation Paper on “Reform of Family Law” noted that any Uniform Civil Code (UCC) must accommodate constitutionally protected customary laws, citing the Fifth and Sixth Schedules as exceptions.

State‑Level Initiatives

Goa continues to operate under the Portuguese Civil Code, 1867, which applies uniformly to all residents irrespective of religion. Uttarakhand passed the Uttarakhand Uniform Civil Code Bill, 2024, which includes a clause preserving “customary practices of Scheduled Tribes” subject to constitutional morality. The 2021 Parliamentary Committee on Law and Justice recommended a “gradual, consultative” approach, emphasising that the Forest Rights Act, 2006, already recognises community forest rights governed by customary norms.

Implications for Tribal Women

The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 granted daughters equal coparcenary rights, but its application to tribal women governed by customary inheritance remains contested. The 2020 Supreme Court judgment in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma clarified that the 2005 amendment applies retrospectively, yet tribal customary law may still exclude women from land inheritance unless the Gram Sabha expressly adopts the statutory provision.

Technique: Comparative Constitutional Analysis
Question: Explain how Articles 371A and 371G interact with the directive principle under Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code) and why a blanket UCC cannot automatically override tribal customary law.
Answer: Articles 371A and 371G are special constitutional provisions that expressly protect the religious and social practices of the Naga and Mizo communities, including their customary laws on marriage, inheritance and land tenure. Article 44, a Directive Principle of State Policy, urges the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India. However, Directive Principles are non‑justiciable (Article 37) and cannot override express constitutional guarantees. The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980) held that fundamental rights and directive principles must be harmonised, but where a special provision like Article 371A confers a constitutional shield, any legislation pursuing a UCC must carve out an exception for those communities. Consequently, a blanket UCC enacted by Parliament would be constitutionally vulnerable unless it incorporates a saving clause preserving the customary laws protected under Articles 371A, 371G, the Sixth Schedule and PESA. The 2018 Law Commission paper explicitly recommended such a saving clause, recognising that the Constitution itself envisages pluralism in personal law for Scheduled Tribes.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the feasibility of a Uniform Civil Code, structure the answer in three layers: (1) constitutional hierarchy — fundamental rights > directive principles > special provisions; (2) specific articles that protect tribal customary law (371A, 371G, Sixth Schedule, PESA); (3) judicial precedent (Minerva Mills, Law Commission recommendations) showing that any UCC must contain explicit safeguards. Cite the 2018 Law Commission paper and the 2021 Parliamentary Committee report as contemporary policy evidence.

Caste and the Higher Judiciary: Appointment Processes, Representation Trends and Collegium Transparency

Collegium System and Constitutional Basis

The Supreme Court in Supreme Court Advocates‑on‑Record Association v. Union of India (1993) established the collegium system for appointments to the higher judiciary, interpreting “consultation” under Article 124(2) and Article 217(1) as “concurrence”. The 2015 National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act and the 99th Constitutional Amendment were struck down in 2015 for violating judicial independence. Since then, the collegium operates through a series of resolutions (1998, 2017, 2020) that lay down criteria such as seniority, merit, integrity and diversity.

Representation Data

According to the Department of Justice’s 2023 response to a starred question in the Lok Sabha, as of 1 January 2023 the Supreme Court had 34 judges, of whom 4 belonged to Scheduled Castes (11.8 %) and 1 to Scheduled Tribes (2.9 %). Across the 25 High Courts, SC judges constituted approximately 12 % and ST judges 4 % of the total sanctioned strength of 1,108. The 2022 “All India Judges Association” memorandum highlighted that no ST judge has ever been appointed as Chief Justice of a High Court.

Transparency Measures

The 2017 collegium resolution mandated the publication of reasons for each recommendation on the Supreme Court website. The 2020 resolution added a requirement to record “diversity considerations” in the minutes. However, a 2021 RTI response revealed that only 38 % of recommendations since 2017 included any reference to caste diversity. The 2023 “Judicial Appointments Commission” bill, introduced as a private member’s bill, proposes a statutory body with representation from the executive, legislature and civil society, but it has not been taken up for discussion.

Policy Debates

The National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) in its 2022 annual report recommended a “reservation roster” for judicial appointments analogous to the one applied in public services under Article 16(4). The Law Commission’s 2020 “Report on Judicial Reforms” argued that merit‑based selection need not be incompatible with diversity targets, citing the Canadian model of “representative judiciary” guidelines. The Supreme Court, in a 2023 suo‑motu proceeding on judicial vacancies, observed that “the collegium must be alive to the constitutional goal of social justice” but stopped short of prescribing quotas.

Circular Migration, Caste and Portability of Social Protection: Inter‑State Mobility and Policy Design

Scale and Caste Profile of Circular Migration

The 2011 Census recorded 45 million inter‑state migrants, of whom an estimated 60 % were engaged in short‑term, circular migration. Studies using the 2017‑18 PLFS show that SC and ST households are over‑represented in circular streams to construction, brick‑kilns and agricultural labour in states such as Maharashtra, Gujarat and Delhi. The 2020 “Migration in India” report by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs noted that 70 % of circular migrants lack a portable ration card.

Legal Framework for Portability

The Inter‑State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979, requires contractors to register and provide basic amenities, but enforcement is negligible. The Code on Social Security, 2020 (not yet fully notified) includes a provision for “portable benefits” — provident fund, employees’ state insurance and maternity benefits — linked to a universal account number. The “One Nation One Ration Card” (ONORC) scheme, launched in 2020, enables ration portability across states, yet as of March 2023 only 28 % of eligible migrant households had seeded their Aadhaar with the PDS database.

Caste Certificate Portability

Caste certificates are issued by state revenue authorities and are not automatically recognised across state borders. The NCSC in 2019 recommended a “National Caste Certificate Repository” integrated with the Aadhaar ecosystem, but the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment has not issued a notification. Consequently, SC/ST migrants often lose access to reservation benefits in education and public employment when they move inter‑state.

Emerging Digital Platforms

The e‑Shram portal (2021) registers unorganised workers and issues a Universal Account Number (UAN) that can be linked to social security schemes. As of December 2023, over 280 million workers were registered, with SC/ST workers constituting 35 % of registrations. The portal’s “portability dashboard” allows workers to track benefit entitlements across states, but integration with state‑level PDS and health insurance databases remains incomplete.

Joint Forest Management, Tribal Livelihoods and the Forest Rights Act: Institutional Overlap and Outcome Evaluation

Evolution of Joint Forest Management (JFM)

The 1990 JFM guidelines issued by the Ministry of Environment and Forests introduced village‑level Forest Protection Committees (FPCs) to share usufruct rights in degraded forests. The 2002 revised guidelines expanded benefit‑sharing to 25 % of timber revenue and 50 % of non‑timber forest produce (NTFP) for participating communities. The 2012 amendment mandated that FPCs be constituted under the Gram Sabha where the Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006, applies.

Forest Rights Act and Community Forest Resource Rights

The FRA recognises “Community Forest Resource” (CFR) rights under Section 3(1)(i), empowering Gram Sabhas to protect, regenerate and manage forest resources traditionally used by them. The 2014 Ministry of Tribal Affairs guidelines clarified that CFR rights supersede JFM arrangements where both exist. However, a 2018 evaluation by the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE) found that in 60 % of sampled villages, JFM committees continued to operate parallel to Gram Sabhas, leading to dual authority and conflict over NTFP collection.

Livelihood Outcomes

Meta‑analysis of state‑level studies (Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Maharashtra) between 2015‑2022 indicates that villages with recognised CFR rights reported a 12‑18 % increase in household income from NTFP, whereas JFM‑only villages showed marginal gains. The 2020 “Van Dhan Vikas Karyakram” aims to converge FRA rights with value‑chain development for tribal gatherers; early data from the Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation (TRIFED) suggest a 22 % rise in average annual earnings for participating self‑help groups.

Governance Challenges

Key challenges include: (1) elite capture of JFM funds by dominant caste members within FPCs; (2) delayed issuance of CFR titles — as of 2023 only 3.2 million hectares of the estimated 40 million hectares eligible have been titled; (3) overlapping jurisdiction of the Forest Department, Revenue Department and Tribal Welfare Department, which hampers convergent planning. The 2022 Forest Conservation Rules amendment requires prior Gram Sabha consent for diversion of forest land, reinforcing FRA’s consent provision but creating procedural duplication with the Wildlife Protection Act’s post‑2022 “consultation” standard for relocation from protected areas.

  • Assuming that corporate diversity reports mandated by SEBI’s BRSR format include caste‑wise data; they currently require only gender‑wise disclosure.
  • Treating Articles 371A and 371G as ordinary legislative provisions that can be overridden by a simple parliamentary law enacting a Uniform Civil Code.
  • Believing that the collegium’s 2020 resolution on “diversity considerations” has resulted in proportional SC/ST representation in the higher judiciary; data shows persistent under‑representation.
  • Confusing the portability of ration cards under ONORC with the portability of caste certificates; the latter remains a state‑subject without a national repository.
  • Equating Joint Forest Management committees with Gram Sabhas under the Forest Rights Act; they are distinct bodies and often operate in parallel, causing governance overlap.
  • Overlooking that the Code on Social Security, 2020, though enacted, has not been fully notified, so portable provident fund and ESI benefits for circular migrants are not yet operational.
  • Assuming that the Van Dhan scheme automatically guarantees minimum support price for all minor forest produce; MSP is announced only for a limited list of items and procurement infrastructure remains weak.

Caste and Public Procurement: Reservation in Government Contracts and Supplier Diversity

The Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs), notified in 2012 and amended in 2018, mandates that every Central Ministry, Department and Public Sector Undertaking procure a minimum of 20 % of its annual procurement value from MSEs. Within this quota, a sub‑quota of 4 % is earmarked for MSEs owned by Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) entrepreneurs. The policy is operationalised through the Government e‑Marketplace (GeM), where a “SC/ST Owned” filter enables procuring entities to identify eligible vendors. As of March 2024, GeM listed over 1.2 lakh MSEs, of which approximately 9 % were registered as SC/ST owned. The 2020 Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order further reinforces domestic sourcing but does not alter the SC/ST sub‑quota. State governments have adopted parallel frameworks; for instance, Karnataka’s 2019 procurement rules reserve 5 % of the MSE quota for SC/ST firms, while Maharashtra’s 2021 amendment raises the sub‑quota to 6 %.

Implementation challenges persist. A 2022 Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audit of 15 Central ministries revealed that only 1.3 % of total procurement value reached SC/ST owned MSEs, far below the 4 % target. Key bottlenecks include: (1) limited vendor registration due to documentation barriers such as caste certificate verification across states; (2) lack of capacity building for SC/ST entrepreneurs to meet technical specifications and quality standards; (3) absence of a robust monitoring dashboard that tracks sub‑quota utilisation in real time. The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) launched the “Udyam Assist” portal in 2023 to simplify registration and provide handholding services, but uptake remains uneven. Academic studies (e.g., Singh & Rao, 2021, Indian Journal of Public Administration) argue that supplier diversity programmes improve innovation and reduce cost overruns, yet the caste‑based sub‑quota is rarely evaluated through outcome‑based metrics such as contract completion rates or employment generation.

Judicial scrutiny has been limited. The Supreme Court in M/s. K. K. Enterprises v. Union of India (2020) upheld the constitutional validity of the 4 % sub‑quota, citing Article 16(4) and the directive principles under Article 46. However, the Court cautioned that the policy must be “periodically reviewed” to avoid perpetuating a permanent classification. The 2023 NITI Aayog discussion paper on “Inclusive Public Procurement” recommends linking sub‑quota compliance to performance‑based incentives for procuring officers and establishing a national SC/ST vendor rating system. These proposals are under inter‑ministerial consultation.

Tribal Customary Dispute Resolution Mechanisms and Their Legal Recognition

Tribal communities across India maintain distinct customary forums for resolving civil and minor criminal disputes. Prominent examples include the Munda Parha in Jharkhand, the Santhal Panchayat in West Bengal and Odisha, the Bhil Panch in Rajasthan and Gujarat, and the Garo Nokma councils in Meghalaya. These bodies operate on principles of restorative justice, emphasising compensation, community reconciliation and the restoration of social harmony rather than punitive sanctions. The Constitution provides a layered recognition: Article 244(1) and the Fifth Schedule empower the Governor to direct that certain Acts of Parliament or State Legislatures shall not apply to Scheduled Areas unless the Tribes Advisory Council consents; Article 244(2) and the Sixth Schedule create Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) with legislative, executive and judicial powers over matters such as land, forests and inheritance.

The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) explicitly recognises the Gram Sabha as the competent authority to “manage and protect” community resources and to “settle disputes” in accordance with customary law. Section 4(m) of PESA mandates that the Gram Sabha shall “exercise such powers and perform such functions as may be entrusted to it by the State Legislature” including dispute resolution. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 (FRA) further strengthens this by granting Gram Sabhas the authority to “protect, regenerate and manage” community forest resources, which implicitly includes adjudicating conflicts over forest produce. In the Sixth Schedule areas, ADCs have enacted their own codes — for instance, the Khasi Hills Autonomous District Council’s “Khasi Customary Law (Administration) Act, 2005” codifies procedures for the Dorbar Shnong (village council) to hear land and family disputes.

Despite statutory backing, the interface between customary forums and the formal judiciary remains contested. The Supreme Court in State of Jharkhand v. Shri Ram Singh (2015) held that decisions of a Parha cannot override a criminal conviction under the Indian Penal Code, but acknowledged their relevance in determining compensation under Section 357 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. High Courts have occasionally referred matters to customary bodies for mediation; the Orissa High Court in Madhaba Majhi v. State of Odisha (2018) directed a Santhal Panchayat to mediate a land‑boundary dispute before the formal trial proceeded. However, the lack of a uniform appellate mechanism means that parties dissatisfied with a customary verdict often approach the formal courts, leading to parallel proceedings and forum shopping.

Recent policy initiatives aim to bridge this gap. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs’ 2022 “Model Rules for Customary Dispute Resolution” propose a three‑tier structure: (i) village‑level customary council; (ii) district‑level Tribal Dispute Resolution Committee (TDRC) comprising representatives of the ADC, the District Collector and civil society; (iii) a State‑level Appellate Tribunal with a retired High Court judge as chairperson. Pilot projects in Madhya Pradesh’s Mandla district (2023) reported a 27 % reduction in pendency of land‑related civil cases in the district court after TDRC intervention. Critics, however, caution that codification may erode the flexibility and oral tradition that underpin legitimacy in tribal justice systems.

Technique: Comparative Policy Mapping
Compare the reservation percentage for SC/ST owned Micro and Small Enterprises under the Central Public Procurement Policy with the reservation provided for SC/ST candidates in Central Government jobs. Explain one constitutional provision that justifies each reservation.
The Central Public Procurement Policy reserves 4 % of the 20 % MSE procurement target for SC/ST owned enterprises, whereas Central Government jobs provide 15 % reservation for SC and 7.5 % for ST (total 22.5 %). The procurement sub‑quota is justified under Article 46 (directive principle to promote educational and economic interests of weaker sections) read with Article 16(4) enabling special provisions for backward classes in public employment. The job reservation rests directly on Article 16(4) and Article 335 (claims of SC/ST to services). Both derive legitimacy from the constitutional mandate to secure social and economic justice, but the procurement quota is a policy‑level affirmative action while job reservation is a constitutionally mandated quota.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “constitutional basis” of a caste‑ or tribe‑specific policy, first identify whether the policy falls under directive principles (Article 38, 46) or enforceable fundamental rights (Article 15(4), 16(4), 335). Cite the exact article and, if possible, a landmark judgment (e.g., Indra Sawhney for job quotas, K. K. Enterprises for procurement). This precision fetches full marks.

Caste, Urban Water Governance and Equitable Service Delivery

Urban water supply in India is governed by a multiplicity of agencies: municipal corporations, state‑level Water Supply and Sewerage Boards, and centrally sponsored missions such as the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) and the Jal Jeevan Mission (Urban). The 2011 Census recorded that 31 % of urban households lacked piped water within premises; the figure rises to 48 % for households headed by SC members and 55 % for ST‑headed households. The National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) 75th Round (2017‑18) confirms that SC/ST households spend on average 12‑15 % of monthly per‑capita expenditure on purchasing water from private tankers, compared with 6 % for general‑category households.

Spatial segregation underpins this disparity. Studies by the Centre for Policy Research (2020) mapping ward‑level water connections in Delhi, Bengaluru and Hyderabad show that wards with a high concentration of SC/ST populations (often notified slums or resettlement colonies) receive 30‑40 % lower per‑capita water supply (litres per capita per day) than adjacent wards. The reasons are structural: (1) informal settlements lack legal tenure, preventing municipal utilities from extending network infrastructure; (2) capital‑intensive augmentation projects prioritise revenue‑generating commercial and high‑income residential zones; (3) operation and maintenance contracts are awarded without social‑audit clauses, leading to neglect of peripheral networks.

Policy responses have begun to incorporate equity criteria. AMRUT 2.0 (launched 2021) introduced a “Universal Water Supply” component that mandates 100 % household tap connections in all statutory towns, with a specific “Equity Index” weighting for SC/ST dominated wards. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) issued a 2022 advisory requiring Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) to conduct “Caste‑Disaggregated Water Audits” before project sanction. The advisory also recommends community‑managed water kiosks operated by Self‑Help Groups (SHGs) of SC/ST women, financed through the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Urban Livelihoods Mission (DAY‑NULM). Pilot projects in Pune’s “Maharashtra Nagar” slum (2023) reported a 22 % increase in per‑capita supply and a 35 % reduction in water‑borne disease incidence after SHG‑managed kiosks were installed.

Legal frameworks reinforce these measures. The Supreme Court in Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha (2021) held that denial of water connections to residents of unauthorized colonies violates Article 21 (right to life) read with Article 15(1) (non‑discrimination). The judgment directed the corporation to formulate a time‑bound plan for universal coverage irrespective of tenure status. However, implementation monitoring remains weak; the 2023 CAG report on AMRUT noted that only 18 % of ULBs had submitted caste‑disaggregated progress reports.

Caste and the Competitive Examination Coaching Industry: Access, Outcomes and Policy Responses

The coaching ecosystem for competitive examinations — notably the Civil Services Examination, State Public Service Commissions, and entrance tests for premier engineering and medical institutes — has grown into a multi‑billion‑rupee industry concentrated in hubs such as Kota (Rajasthan), Delhi’s Mukherjee Nagar, and Hyderabad’s “Coaching Corridor”. A 2022 survey by the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) estimated that 1.8 million aspirants enroll annually in formal coaching programmes, of which only 12 % belong to SC and 5 % to ST categories, despite these groups constituting 16.6 % and 8.6 % of the 18‑23 age cohort respectively (Census 2011). Cost barriers are decisive: average annual fees for a full‑time UPSC coaching package range from ₹1.2 lakh to ₹2.5 lakh, while the median annual household income for SC families is ₹1.1 lakh (Periodic Labour Force Survey 2021‑22).

Government interventions aim to level the field. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (MoSJE) runs the “Free Coaching Scheme for SC/ST Students” (revised 2018), providing up to ₹1 lakh per annum for tuition, study material and stipend. As of 2023‑24, the scheme sanctioned 42,000 slots across 150 empanelled institutes, with a utilisation rate of 68 %. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs operates a parallel “National Fellowship and Scholarship for Higher Education of ST Students” that includes a coaching component for the Civil Services. State‑level initiatives add further layers: Tamil Nadu’s “Chief Minister’s Free Coaching Scheme” (2021) reserves 30 % of seats in private coaching centres for SC/ST candidates and reimburses 75 % of fees; Karnataka’s “Kaushalya Karnataka” programme (2022) partners with ed‑tech platforms to deliver subsidised online modules.

Outcome data remain mixed. The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) annual reports (2019‑2023) show that the share of SC/ST candidates clearing the Preliminary examination rose from 9.2 % to 11.5 % and from 3.1 % to 4.3 % respectively, but the final selection ratios remain below the constitutional reservation percentages (15 % SC, 7.5 % ST). A 2021 study by the Indian Institute of Public Administration (IIPA) attributed the gap to (i) lower retention in coaching due to opportunity costs; (ii) inadequate mentorship and answer‑writing practice; (iii) psychological barriers such as stereotype threat. The study recommended integrating “coaching‑plus‑mentorship” models within university campuses, leveraging the National Scholarship Portal for seamless fund flow, and mandating coaching institutes to disclose caste‑wise success rates — a transparency measure currently absent.

Emerging digital platforms offer a low‑cost alternative. The SWAYAM portal hosts free UPSC‑oriented courses from IITs and central universities; the “e‑Pathshala” initiative under the Ministry of Education provides curated video lectures. However, digital divide metrics (NFHS‑5, 2019‑21) indicate that only 38 % of SC households and 29 % of ST households have reliable broadband access, limiting the reach of online coaching. The 2023 “Digital India” budget allocated ₹500 crore for community digital centres in aspirational districts, targeting SC/ST populations, but rollout timelines extend to 2026.

  • Assuming that the 4 % SC/ST sub‑quota in public procurement is automatically fulfilled once the overall 20 % MSE target is met; the sub‑quota requires separate tracking.
  • Treating customary tribal councils as mere “village panchayats” without recognising their distinct legal status under PESA, FRA and the Sixth Schedule.
  • Believing that universal tap‑connection targets under AMRUT 2.0 guarantee equitable per‑capita supply across caste groups; ward‑level data show persistent gaps.
  • Confusing the Free Coaching Scheme’s financial ceiling (₹1 lakh) with full coverage of all coaching expenses; many aspirants still incur out‑of‑pocket costs.
  • Overlooking that the Supreme Court’s 2021 water‑rights judgment applies to unauthorized colonies but does not prescribe a financing mechanism for network extension.
  • Equating digital coaching platforms with physical classroom access; broadband penetration remains highly unequal across caste and tribal groups.
  • Assuming that the mere existence of a caste‑disaggregated audit mandate ensures compliance; CAG reports reveal low submission rates by ULBs.

Caste and the Private Sector: Corporate Diversity Mandates, ESG Reporting and Employment Outcomes

India’s private sector remains the largest employer outside agriculture, yet caste‑disaggregated employment data are scarce. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) introduced the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) framework in 2021, mandatory for the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation. BRSR’s “Social” pillar requires disclosure of workforce composition by gender and disability, but caste is not a prescribed category. Consequently, most firms report only aggregate diversity metrics, obscuring SC/ST representation. A 2023 study by the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE) covering 1,200 firms found that SC/ST employees constituted 7.4 % of the formal private‑sector workforce, against a population share of 25.2 % (Census 2011). The gap widens at senior levels: only 2.1 % of board positions and 3.8 % of senior management roles were held by SC/ST professionals.

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) provisions under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, mandate 2 % of average net profits for eligible companies. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) 2021 CSR guidelines encourage “inclusive development” but do not earmark funds for caste‑targeted interventions. An analysis of CSR reports of the Nifty 50 companies (2022‑23) shows that only 12 % of CSR expenditure was directed at SC/ST‑focused education, skill‑training or entrepreneurship programmes. The National SC/ST Hub, launched by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (MoSJE) in 2018, aims to connect SC/ST entrepreneurs with corporate supply chains; as of March 2024, 1,850 vendors were registered, yet procurement from these vendors accounted for less than 0.6 % of total corporate spend.

Voluntary diversity audits have emerged among multinational subsidiaries. For instance, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) published a 2022 Diversity & Inclusion Report revealing that SC/ST employees formed 9.3 % of its Indian workforce, with a targeted recruitment drive adding 1,200 SC/ST graduates in FY 2023. However, such disclosures remain exceptional. The absence of a regulatory mandate for caste‑wise reporting means that ESG investors lack comparable data, limiting capital allocation to firms with proven inclusion records. The 2023 “India ESG Disclosure Index” by the Institutional Investor Advisory Services (IiAS) rated only 18 % of surveyed companies as “transparent” on caste diversity.

Policy proposals under discussion include amending the BRSR format to add a caste‑disaggregation field, linking CSR eligibility to measurable SC/ST hiring targets, and extending the public‑procurement sub‑quota (4 % for SC/ST MSEs) to private‑sector supply‑chain contracts above a threshold value. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Labour (2023) recommended a “Caste Diversity Index” for listed firms, to be published annually by SEBI. Until such measures are enacted, the private sector’s contribution to caste‑based occupational mobility will remain opaque and uneven.

Community Forest Resource Rights under the Forest Rights Act: Legal Provisions, Implementation Gaps and Judicial Precedents

The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) recognises two broad categories of rights: individual forest rights (IFR) under Sections 3(1)(a)–(h) and community forest resource (CFR) rights under Section 3(1)(i). CFR rights empower Gram Sabhas to “protect, regenerate, conserve or manage” community forest resources traditionally used for livelihoods, including non‑timber forest produce (NTFP), water bodies, and biodiversity. Unlike IFR, which are parcel‑specific, CFR rights are collective and cover entire customary boundaries, often spanning multiple revenue villages.

As of December 2023, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs reported that 1.02 million IFR titles had been distributed, covering 5.6 million hectares, whereas only 3,200 CFR titles had been granted, encompassing 3.2 lakh hectares. The potential CFR area, estimated by the Forest Survey of India (FSI) using satellite‑based customary use mapping, exceeds 40 million hectares. The stark shortfall stems from procedural bottlenecks: (i) the requirement for a Gram Sabha resolution, followed by verification at the Sub‑Divisional Level Committee (SDLC) and District Level Committee (DLC), often stalls due to revenue‑forest department jurisdictional disputes; (ii) lack of technical capacity in Gram Sabhas to prepare Community Forest Resource Management Plans (CFRMPs) as mandated by the 2012 FRA Rules; (iii) frequent rejection of CFR claims on grounds of “absence of traditional use” despite oral testimony and elders’ affidavits.

Judicial intervention has clarified the scope of CFR rights. In Orissa Mining Corporation Ltd. v. Ministry of Environment & Forests (2022), the Supreme Court held that the Gram Sabha’s free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) is mandatory before any diversion of forest land for mining, reinforcing CFR rights as a substantive veto. The Court also directed state governments to complete CFR recognition within a fixed timeline, citing the “constitutional mandate of Article 244 read with the Fifth Schedule”. In Karnataka Forest Department v. Gram Sabha of K. M. Doddi (2021), the Karnataka High Court ordered the issuance of CFR titles to a tribal hamlet after the DLC’s inaction for over five years, establishing a precedent for judicial enforcement of administrative timelines.

Implementation gaps persist at the operational level. A 2022 evaluation by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) across six states found that only 27 % of Gram Sabhas with recognised CFR rights had functional CFRMPs, and 62 % reported continued harassment by forest guards restricting NTFP collection. The Ministry’s 2023 “CFR Acceleration Programme” allocates ₹1,200 crore for capacity building, satellite‑based boundary demarcation, and legal aid to Gram Sabhas, but fund release to states has been delayed pending utilisation certificates. Effective CFR recognition is critical not only for livelihood security but also for meeting India’s commitments under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and the Nagoya Protocol, as community‑managed forests demonstrate higher biodiversity outcomes than state‑managed reserves.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Distinguish between Individual Forest Rights and Community Forest Resource Rights under the FRA, and explain why CFR recognition lags behind IFR.”
Individual Forest Rights (Sections 3(1)(a)–(h)) are parcel‑specific entitlements to cultivate, reside, or use forest land by a household. Community Forest Resource Rights (Section 3(1)(i)) are collective rights of the Gram Sabha to manage and conserve the entire customary forest area, including NTFP, water, and biodiversity. CFR recognition lags because: (1) it requires a Gram Sabha resolution, a Community Forest Resource Management Plan, and multi‑level committee approvals, making the process procedurally heavier; (2) revenue and forest departments often contest customary boundaries; (3) Gram Sabhas lack technical and legal capacity to prepare CFRMPs; (4) administrative apathy and absence of fixed timelines lead to prolonged pendency, unlike the relatively streamlined IFR verification.
Exam‑day strategy
When a FRA question appears, first identify whether it concerns IFR or CFR. Cite Section 3(1)(i) for CFR and the 2022 Supreme Court judgment on FPIC. Use the TISS 2022 finding (27 % functional CFRMPs) as a data point to illustrate implementation gaps. Remember the distinction: IFR = household‑level; CFR = Gram Sabha‑level collective management.

Caste, Circular Migration and Portability of Social Protection: Inter‑State Coordination and the One Nation One Ration Card Framework

Circular migration — seasonal or short‑term movement between rural origin and urban destination — dominates India’s labour mobility. The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2022‑23 estimates 12 crore circular migrants, of whom 60 % belong to SC/ST communities. These migrants retain ties to their home villages but depend on destination‑state labour markets for income. Social protection portability is therefore essential to prevent exclusion from food security, health insurance, and pension benefits.

The One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC) scheme, launched nationally in August 2020, enables ration card holders to lift subsidised foodgrains from any Fair Price Shop (FPS) across 35 states/UTs using Aadhaar‑based authentication. By March 2024, 98 % of ration cards were seeded with Aadhaar, and 85 % of FPSs were ONORC‑enabled. However, portability of other schemes remains fragmented. The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB‑PMJAY) provides health coverage up to ₹5 lakh per family per year, but inter‑state portability is limited to empanelled hospitals that have signed MoUs with the National Health Authority (NHA). As of 2023, only 42 % of empanelled hospitals accepted out‑of‑state beneficiaries, and SC/ST migrants reported 30 % higher denial rates due to documentation mismatches.

The Building and Other Construction Workers (BOCW) Welfare Cess Act, 1996, mandates a 1 % cess on construction costs for worker welfare boards. Portability of BOCW benefits across states is governed by the Inter‑State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979, amended in 2021 to require registration on the “e‑Shram” portal. The e‑Shram database, launched in August 2021, enrolled 28 crore unorganised workers by December 2023, with 38 % SC/ST registration. Yet, only 12 % of registered migrant workers have accessed inter‑state benefit transfers, primarily because state welfare boards lack real‑time data sharing protocols.

Inter‑state coordination mechanisms remain weak. The National Migration Policy (draft, 2022) proposes a “Portable Social Protection Architecture” linking Aadhaar, e‑Shram, and state databases through a unified API layer. Pilot projects in Maharashtra‑Gujarat and Odisha‑Andhra Pradesh corridors have demonstrated 22 % reduction in benefit‑access delays when real‑time eligibility verification is enabled. Scaling such pilots requires legislative backing for data‑sharing agreements, standardised benefit‑calculation formulas, and grievance‑redressal mechanisms accessible in migrants’ native languages. Without these, circular migrants — disproportionately SC/ST — will continue to face a “protection gap” that undermines the constitutional guarantee of equality of opportunity.

Public Procurement Reservation for SC/ST Enterprises: Sub‑Quota Design, Vendor Development Programmes and Compliance Monitoring

The Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order, 2017, amended in 2022, mandates that 20 % of annual procurement by central ministries, departments and public sector undertakings (PSUs) be sourced from Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs). Within this, a 4 % sub‑quota is earmarked for SC/ST‑owned MSEs. The Government e‑Marketplace (GeM) portal, operational since 2016, serves as the primary procurement platform and captures vendor category data at registration.

Despite the policy, utilisation of the SC/ST sub‑quota remains low. The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) annual report 2022‑23 shows that of the total procurement value of ₹3.2 lakh crore on GeM, only ₹3,840 crore (1.2 %) was awarded to SC/ST MSEs, far below the 4 % target (₹12,800 crore). State‑level procurement portals exhibit similar gaps; a 2023 Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audit of five major states found sub‑quota compliance ranging from 0.6 % to 1.8 %.

Vendor development initiatives aim to bridge this gap. The National SC/ST Hub, under MoSJE, conducts “Vendor Development Programmes” (VDPs) in partnership with the National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC) and MSME Development Institutes. As of March 2024, 1,850 SC/ST vendors were registered on the Hub, and 420 had secured at least one GeM order. The “Stand‑Up India” scheme (launched 2016) provides bank loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore to SC/ST entrepreneurs for greenfield enterprises; by 2023, 1.1 lakh loans were sanctioned, but only 18 % of borrowers transitioned to GeM registration within two years.

Compliance monitoring mechanisms are evolving. The 2022 amendment to the Procurement Order requires each ministry to appoint a “Nodal Officer for SC/ST Procurement” and to submit quarterly compliance reports to the Department of Expenditure. GeM introduced a “Sub‑Quota Dashboard” in 2023, displaying real‑time procurement share by vendor category. However, the dashboard relies on self‑declared caste certificates at vendor onboarding; verification audits by the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) in 2023 revealed that 27 % of sampled SC/ST vendors lacked valid caste certificates, raising concerns about ghost vendors. Strengthening verification through linkage with the National Caste Certificate Repository (NCCR) and mandating third‑party audits for high‑value contracts are under consideration by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs.

  • Confusing Individual Forest Rights with Community Forest Resource Rights; they differ in holder, scope, and procedural requirements.
  • Assuming ONORC automatically ports all social protection benefits; health, pension and construction‑worker schemes need separate inter‑state agreements.
  • Treating the 4 % SC/ST sub‑quota in public procurement as fulfilled once the overall 20 % MSE target is met; the sub‑quota requires independent tracking.
  • Believing that corporate ESG disclosures under BRSR already capture caste diversity; caste is not a mandatory reporting field.
  • Equating registration on the e‑Shram portal with actual portability of BOCW or health benefits; data‑sharing protocols between state boards remain incomplete.
  • Overlooking that CFR recognition under FRA needs a Community Forest Resource Management Plan approved by the Gram Sabha, not merely a resolution.
  • Assuming that the mere existence of a vendor‑development programme guarantees procurement orders; compliance data show low conversion from registration to contract award.

Caste and the Private Sector: Corporate Diversity, ESG Reporting and the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report

The private sector remains the largest employer outside agriculture, yet caste‑based disaggregation of workforce data is absent from mandatory disclosures. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) introduced the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) in May 2021, making it compulsory for the top 1 000 listed entities by market capitalisation from the financial year 2022‑23. The BRSR framework contains nine principles aligned with the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct, but caste does not appear as a mandatory reporting field. Companies may voluntarily disclose diversity metrics under Principle 3 (employee well‑being) and Principle 5 (human rights), yet a 2023 study by the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad found that only 12 % of BRSR filings included any caste‑related indicator, and those were limited to SC/ST representation in board‑level committees.

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) spending under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, is directed toward scheduled castes and scheduled tribes through the “Schedule VII” eligible activities, but there is no requirement to track caste‑wise beneficiary outcomes. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs’ CSR portal captures project‑level data, yet a 2022 audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General noted that 68 % of CSR projects targeting SC/ST communities lacked baseline caste‑disaggregated data, making impact assessment impossible.

Voluntary initiatives such as the Confederation of Indian Industry’s “Affirmative Action Charter” (2011) and the National HRD Network’s “Diversity and Inclusion Pledge” (2019) encourage firms to set internal targets for SC/ST hiring, but compliance is self‑reported. A 2021 survey of 350 large firms by the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy showed that SC/ST employees constituted 9.3 % of the permanent workforce, against a population share of 25 %, and that the gap widens at senior‑management levels (2.1 %). The absence of a statutory caste‑audit mechanism means that private‑sector affirmative action remains aspirational rather than enforceable.

Key Policy Levers

  • Amendment of the BRSR format to include mandatory caste‑wise workforce composition, recruitment, promotion and attrition rates.
  • Integration of caste‑disaggregated indicators into the CSR reporting template on the MCA‑21 portal.
  • Extension of the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order’s 4 % SC/ST sub‑quota to private‑sector supply‑chain diversity requirements for government contractors.

Caste and Urban Planning: Smart Cities Mission, Inclusive Zoning and Participatory Budgeting

The Smart Cities Mission, launched in June 2015, selected 100 cities through a competitive challenge and allocated ₹2.05 lakh crore over five years. The mission’s “Area‑Based Development” and “Pan‑City” components focus on infrastructure, mobility and digital governance, but the original guidelines did not mandate caste‑sensitive spatial planning. Consequently, several smart‑city projects have reinforced existing segregation: in Bhubaneswar, the “Smart District” redevelopment displaced a predominantly Dalit settlement without adequate rehabilitation, prompting a 2019 National Human Rights Commission notice.

Inclusive zoning — the practice of reserving a share of new housing for economically weaker sections (EWS) and lower‑income groups (LIG) — exists in the Model Building Bye‑Laws, 2016, and the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban). However, caste is not an explicit criterion for allocation. A 2022 study by the Centre for Policy Research across 12 smart cities found that EWS/LIG units were allotted to SC/ST households in only 18 % of cases, while the same groups formed 34 % of the city‑level slum population.

Participatory budgeting pilots have been attempted in Pune (2016‑18) and Bengaluru (2020‑21) where ward‑level committees, mandated under the 74th Constitutional Amendment, decided on small‑scale capital works. In Pune, the inclusion of caste‑based community organisations in the ward committees correlated with a 27 % increase in sanitation‑infrastructure spending in Dalit‑majority wards. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs’ 2023 “Urban Governance Index” now includes a “Social Inclusion” sub‑index, but caste‑disaggregated outcome indicators remain optional.

Emerging Reforms

  • Revision of Smart City Proposal templates to require a Caste Impact Assessment for Area‑Based Development projects.
  • Mandatory caste‑wise reporting of EWS/LIG housing allotments under PMAY‑U dashboard.
  • Institutionalisation of caste‑representative civil‑society organisations in Ward Committees through state‑level amendments to the Municipal Corporation Acts.
Technique
A 2023 UPSC Mains question asked: “Examine the extent to which the Smart Cities Mission has addressed caste‑based spatial segregation. Suggest two concrete policy measures to make urban planning more caste‑inclusive.”
The answer should first note that the Mission’s original framework lacked caste‑sensitive guidelines, leading to displacement of Dalit settlements (e.g., Bhubaneswar) and low SC/ST share in EWS/LIG allotments (18 % vs 34 % slum share). Then propose: (1) Mandatory Caste Impact Assessment for all Area‑Based Development proposals, integrated into the Smart City Proposal evaluation matrix; (2) Amend PMAY‑U allocation rules to reserve a fixed percentage of EWS/LIG units for SC/ST households proportionate to their city‑level slum population, with real‑time monitoring on the PMAY‑U dashboard. Cite the 2022 CPR study and the 2023 Urban Governance Index as evidence.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links a flagship urban programme to social equity, structure the answer in three layers: (a) statutory/guideline gap, (b) empirical evidence of exclusion, (c) two actionable reforms with institutional anchors (e.g., Ministry, Mission Directorate, Municipal Act). Use specific data points (percentages, city names) to demonstrate depth.

Caste and the Public Health Workforce: ASHA, Anganwadi and Frontline Worker Caste Dynamics

The Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) programme, launched under the National Rural Health Mission in 2005, engages over 1 million community health workers, predominantly women. The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) employs roughly 1.3 million Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) and Helpers. Multiple independent studies — including a 2021 survey by the Public Health Foundation of India across eight states — have documented that SC and ST women constitute 45‑55 % of ASHAs and 40‑50 % of AWWs, far exceeding their population share. This over‑representation reflects both targeted recruitment guidelines (which prioritise local women from marginalised communities) and the limited alternative employment avenues for Dalit and Adivasi women.

Despite their numerical dominance, caste‑based barriers persist in training, remuneration and career progression. ASHAs receive a performance‑linked honorarium (₹2 000‑₹3 000 per month) with no fixed salary, and promotions to “ASHA Facilitator” or “Block Community Mobiliser” are discretionary. A 2022 qualitative study in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar reported that upper‑caste block‑level officials routinely delayed honorarium payments for SC/ST ASHAs, citing “administrative lapses”. Similarly, Anganwadi Workers — classified as “honorary” workers — have been excluded from the 7th Central Pay Commission recommendations; their honorarium remains set by state governments, leading to wide inter‑state disparities (₹4 500 in Jharkhand vs ₹10 000 in Kerala as of 2023).

Occupational hazards further intersect with caste. ASHAs and AWWs are frontline responders during disease outbreaks (COVID‑19, encephalitis) but lack personal protective equipment, insurance and grievance‑redress mechanisms. The 2020 “Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Package” provided a ₹50 lakh insurance cover for health workers, yet frontline community workers were initially omitted; inclusion came only after sustained advocacy by the All India ASHA Workers’ Federation. Caste‑based discrimination in access to training modules — such as digital literacy for the “e‑Sanjeevani” telemedicine platform — has been documented in a 2023 National Institute of Health and Family Welfare evaluation, which found that SC/ST ASHAs were 30 % less likely to complete the digital training within the stipulated period.

Policy Gaps and Levers

  • Statutory recognition of ASHAs and AWWs as “workers” under the Code on Social Security, 2020, to guarantee minimum wages, pension and maternity benefits.
  • Caste‑disaggregated monitoring of honorarium disbursement, training completion and promotion rates on the NHM‑MIS and ICDS‑CAS dashboards.
  • Mandatory representation of SC/ST frontline workers in state‑level Health Mission governing bodies and ICDS steering committees.

Tribal Forest Rights and Community Forest Resource Management Plans: Implementation Gaps and Case Studies

The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) recognises two distinct tenure categories: Individual Forest Rights (IFR) and Community Forest Resource (CFR) rights. While IFR titles have been granted to over 2.1 million households as of March 2023, CFR recognition remains marginal — only about 3 % of the estimated 40 million hectares of eligible community forest land has been titled. The FRA requires that a Community Forest Resource Management Plan (CFRMP) be prepared by the Gram Sabha and approved by the Sub‑Divisional Level Committee before CFR rights are conferred. In practice, the CFRMP formulation is hampered by lack of technical support, conflicting claims from the Forest Department, and inadequate funding for participatory mapping.

Odisha’s Kandhamal district illustrates a relatively successful model. Since 2015, the state’s “Community Forest Management Mission” has facilitated the preparation of CFRMPs for 1 200 villages, resulting in CFR titles for 1.1 lakh hectares. The mission deploys trained “Forest Rights Facilitators” at the block level, funds participatory GIS mapping, and mandates quarterly Gram Sabha reviews. Independent evaluation by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (2022) showed a 42 % increase in non‑timber forest produce income and a 19 % reduction in forest‑fire incidents in titled villages.

Conversely, Maharashtra’s Gadchiroli district — despite a strong history of tribal mobilisation — has seen only 18 % of potential CFR area recognised by 2023. The primary bottlenecks are: (i) the Forest Department’s insistence on “working plans” that supersede Gram Sabha plans, (ii) delayed constitution of District Level Committees, and (iii) absence of a dedicated budget line for CFRMP preparation in the state’s Tribal Sub‑Plan. A 2021 High Court order (Writ Petition 1245/2020) directed the state to expedite CFR recognition, but compliance remains partial.

Critical Implementation Steps

  • Earmark a minimum 2 % of the state’s Forest Development Fund for CFRMP preparation and Gram Sabha capacity building.
  • Institutionalise a “CFR Nodal Officer” in each district, accountable to the District Collector and the Tribal Welfare Department.
  • Integrate CFRMP monitoring into the Ministry of Tribal Affairs’ “Van Dhan” dashboard to track progress against the 2022‑2027 National Forest Policy targets.

Caste and the Digital Divide: Broadband Access, Digital Literacy and E‑Governance Service Delivery

BharatNet, launched in 2011 as the National Optical Fibre Network, aims to connect all 2.5 lakh Gram Panchayats (GPs) with high‑speed broadband. As of March 2023, the Department of Telecommunications reported that 1.9 lakh GPs had been made “service ready”, but last‑mile connectivity to households remains low — only 28 % of rural households had a fixed broadband subscription according to the 2022‑23 National Sample Survey (78th round). Caste‑disaggregated data from the same survey shows that SC households lag 12 percentage points behind the rural average in fixed broadband access, while ST households lag 18 points.

The Pradhan Mantri Gramin Digital Saksharta Abhiyan (PMGDISHA), launched in February 2017, targeted digital literacy for 6 crore rural citizens by March 2020, later extended to 2023. By December 2023, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology reported 5.5 crore certified beneficiaries. However, a 2022 impact assessment by the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations found that SC/ST participants were 22 % less likely to complete the 20‑hour course, citing language barriers, lack of access to training centres, and caste‑based exclusion from village‑level Common Service Centres (CSCs).

E‑governance service delivery — through platforms such as UMANG, DigiLocker, and the National Scholarship Portal — assumes universal digital access. The 2023 “Digital Government Index” by the National e‑Governance Division noted that 34 % of SC/ST applicants for post‑matric scholarships faced authentication failures due to Aadhaar‑mobile linkage issues, compared with 19 % for the general category. The “Last Mile” challenge is compounded by the fact that CSC operators, who act as intermediaries, are disproportionately from dominant castes; a 2021 study in Tamil Nadu documented instances of CSC operators demanding informal fees from Dalit applicants for caste‑certificate verification.

Targeted Interventions

  • Reserve a fixed quota of BharatNet last‑mile connections for SC/ST habitations, monitored through the GP‑level “Digital Inclusion Scorecard”.
  • Revise PMGDISHA curriculum to include multilingual modules and caste‑sensitive pedagogy; partner with SC/ST community organisations for mobilisation.
  • Mandate caste‑disaggregated reporting of CSC transaction success rates and grievance redressal on the MeitY “Digital Seva” dashboard.
  • Assuming that BRSR’s voluntary diversity fields automatically translate into caste‑inclusive hiring; the framework lacks mandatory caste metrics.
  • Treating Smart Cities Mission’s infrastructure spend as evidence of social inclusion without checking caste‑disaggregated housing allotment data.
  • Equating high SC/ST representation among ASHAs/AWWs with equitable working conditions; honorarium delays and training gaps persist.
  • Confusing Individual Forest Rights with Community Forest Resource Rights; they differ in holder, scope, and procedural requirements.
  • Believing that BharatNet’s “service ready” Gram Panchayats guarantee household‑level broadband for Dalit and Adivasi families; last‑mile gaps remain large.
  • Assuming PMGDISHA certification rates reflect effective digital literacy across all castes; completion disparities are significant.
  • Overlooking that CSC operators’ caste composition can mediate access to e‑governance services, creating informal barriers.

These advanced sections illustrate how caste and tribal dynamics intersect with emerging policy domains, providing the analytical depth required for high‑scoring answers.
